extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluation criteria for invoking the AIA prior-art exception under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) based on common ownership or a joint research agreement, including required statements, evidence, timing, and related procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) prior-art exception may be invoked only for disclosures applied as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) (disclosures in U.S. patents, U.S. patent applications, or WIPO published international applications). The exception applies when the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) (anticipation) or 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AIA expanded the previous CREATE Act exception to apply to anticipation (102(a)(2)) as well as obviousness. The exception does NOT apply to disclosures that qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) (public disclosures), i.e., a disclosure that is prior art under 102(a)(1) cannot be excepted by 102(b)(2)(C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership must exist not later than the effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership (or an obligation to assign both the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention to the same person/organization) must exist not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention for 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of present common ownership filed after the effective filing date is not sufficient (unless it was filed on the effective filing date). Actual ownership or a legal, enforceable obligation to assign must exist by the effective filing date; moral or unenforceable obligations are insufficient. Retention of basic ownership rights (e.g., a license where owner retains ownership) does not defeat ownership for these purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed statement to establish common ownership (content & form)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant or patent owner may establish common ownership by submitting a clear, conspicuous, signed statement (signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b)) that the application and the subject matter disclosed in the reference were, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, owned by or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person(s) or organization(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on a separate paper or separate labeled section) so the examiner notices it. Example wording provided in the MPEP is sufficient. The statement may be made by the applicant/patent owner or their representative and is ordinarily sufficient because of the applicant’s paramount obligation of candor and good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional objective evidence to support common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants/patent owners may, but are not required to, submit objective evidence supporting the statement of common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of objective evidence include: (A) reference to assignments recorded in the USPTO (37 CFR Part 3) conveying the entire rights to the same person/organization; (B) copies of unrecorded assignments filed in each application; (C) an affidavit or declaration by the common owner stating facts explaining the belief in common ownership and properly signed by an empowered official; and (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response when independent evidence raises doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: If independent evidence raises a material doubt about the accuracy of the applicant’s/patent owner’s representation of common ownership or of an obligation to assign, the examiner should explain the doubt and may require objective evidence of common ownership (or obligation to assign) as of the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent evidence might show lack of common ownership; in such cases the examiner may require assignments, affidavits, court decisions, or other objective proof. Examiners should note that execution dates in assignment documents may not reflect the date a party was under an obligation to assign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement (JRA) invocation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke the JRA provisions (35 U.S.C. 102(c)) for the 102(b)(2)(C) exception, the applicant/patent owner must provide a statement that (1) the subject matter and the claimed invention were developed or made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement (within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 100(h) and 37 CFR 1.9(e)); (2) the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; and (3) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)). The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the names of the parties to the JRA are not in the application, the application must be amended to include them (see 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1)). The applicant may but is not required to file additional evidence supporting the existence of the JRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.71(g) amendment requirements and timing for JRA party names
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification may be amended under 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1) to disclose the names of the parties to a joint research agreement; such an amendment may require a processing fee under 37 CFR 1.17(i) if not filed within specified time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time windows when the fee is not required include: (i) within three months of the filing date of a national application; (ii) within three months of the date of entry of the national stage in an international application; (iii) before mailing of a first Office action on the merits; or (iv) before the mailing of a first Office action after filing a request for continued examination (RCE) under 37 CFR 1.114. If the amendment is filed after the issue fee is paid and the issued patent does not include the names, the patent must be corrected by a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323 for the amendment to be effective. It is unnecessary to file a reissue application or request for reexamination solely to submit such an amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer / entry refusal and effect on prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment under 37 CFR 1.71(g) submitted to overcome a rejection based on a U.S. patent (available only under 102(a)(2)) may be refused entry by the examiner if not accompanied by an appropriate terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(d), because the amendment may necessitate reopening prosecution (e.g., entry of a double patenting rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner withdraws the rejection upon entry of the amendment, the examiner may need to issue a new double patenting rejection based on the excepted subject matter; such an Office action can be made final provided no other new ground of rejection not necessitated by the amendment or an IDS during the 37 CFR 1.97(c) period is introduced. The Office action may be final even if the claims were not amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural form & signature requirements for statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements invoking common ownership or a JRA must meet the procedural form and signature rules: they should be clear and conspicuous, on or begin on a separate sheet, not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP provides example wording. Representatives of record have the best knowledge and their signed statement is ordinarily sufficient. Failure to follow form/signature requirements may render the statement deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the 102(b)(2)(C) exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the 102(b)(2)(C) exception is properly invoked, it only disqualifies the disclosure as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2); it does not (1) except disclosures that are prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1), (2) remove the disclosure as a basis for double patenting rejections, or (3) remove the disclosure as evidence of enablement or inherency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excepted disclosures may still be used as the basis for statutory or nonstatutory double patenting rejections (see MPEP § 804) and may still serve as evidence for enablement/inherency issues (see MPEP § 2131.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and effects of a proper invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of unpatentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103, the burden to overcome the rejection by invoking 102(b)(2)(C) (via common ownership or JRA) rests on the applicant/patentee. If the exception is properly invoked following the rules, the examiner will treat the application and the excepted subject matter as if owned by the same person for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after proper invocation, the excepted subject matter may still be used for double patenting or other purposes noted in the MPEP. Applicants may submit supporting evidence but are not required to do so unless the examiner raises a material doubt.
